section.title: The Twelve and the True Family
section.sectionRationale: The conflict reaches a first climax and a first turning. Jesus heals a withered hand on the Sabbath, and His enemies begin plotting His death. Crowds press from every direction, He appoints the Twelve, and then two shocking verdicts fall: His own family says He is out of His mind, and the scribes say He is possessed. Jesus answers with the parable of the strong man and the warning about blaspheming the Spirit, and redefines His true family as those who do God's will.
section.thesis: Jesus is neither mad nor demonic but the stronger One who has come to bind Satan and plunder his house, and those who receive Him, doing the will of God, become His true family, while those who call the Spirit's work demonic cut themselves off from forgiveness.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the withered hand and the death plot; the crowds and the unclean spirits; the appointing of the Twelve; the charge of madness and the Beelzebul controversy; and the true family of Jesus.

units.label: The withered hand and the death plot
units.note: to do good or to do evil on the Sabbath

verses.text: Once again Jesus entered the synagogue, and a man with a withered hand was there.
In order to accuse Jesus, they were watching to see if He would heal on the Sabbath.
Then Jesus said to the man with the withered hand, “Stand up among us.”
And He asked them, “Which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?” But they were silent.
Jesus looked around at them with anger and sorrow at their hardness of heart. Then He said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” So he stretched it out, and it was restored.
At this, the Pharisees went out and began plotting with the Herodians how they might kill Jesus.

units.label: The crowds and the unclean spirits
units.note: You are the Son of God

verses.text: So Jesus withdrew with His disciples to the sea, accompanied by a large crowd from Galilee, Judea,
Jerusalem, Idumea, the region beyond the Jordan, and the vicinity of Tyre and Sidon. The large crowd came to Him when they heard what great things He was doing.
Jesus asked His disciples to have a boat ready for Him so that the crowd would not crush Him.
For He had healed so many that all who had diseases were pressing forward to touch Him.
And when the unclean spirits saw Him, they fell down before Him and cried out, “You are the Son of God!”
But He warned them sternly not to make Him known.

units.label: The appointing of the Twelve
units.note: to be with Him and to be sent out

verses.text: Then Jesus went up on the mountain and called for those He wanted, and they came to Him.
He appointed twelve of them, whom He designated as {{apostolos|apostles}}, to accompany Him, to be sent out to preach,
and to have authority to drive out demons.
These are the twelve He appointed: Simon (whom He named Peter),
James son of Zebedee and his brother John (whom He named Boanerges, meaning “Sons of Thunder”),
Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot,
and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus.

units.label: Madness or the strong man bound
units.note: how can Satan drive out Satan

verses.text: Then Jesus went home, and once again a crowd gathered, so that He and His disciples could not even eat.
When His family heard about this, they went out to take custody of Him, saying, “He is out of His mind.”
And the scribes who had come down from Jerusalem were saying, “He is possessed by Beelzebul,” and, “By the prince of the demons He drives out demons.”
So Jesus called them together and began to speak to them in parables: “How can Satan drive out Satan?
If a kingdom is divided against itself, it cannot stand.
If a house is divided against itself, it cannot stand.
And if Satan is divided and rises against himself, he cannot stand; his end has come.
Indeed, no one can enter a {{ischyros|strong man}}’s house to steal his possessions unless he first ties up the strong man. Then he can plunder his house.
Truly I tell you, the sons of men will be forgiven all sins and blasphemies, as many as they utter.
But whoever {{blasphemia|blasphemes}} against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven; he is guilty of eternal sin.”
Jesus made this statement because they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.”

units.label: The true family of Jesus
units.note: whoever does the will of God

verses.text: Then Jesus’ mother and brothers came and stood outside. They sent someone in to summon Him,
and a crowd was sitting around Him. “Look,” He was told, “Your mother and brothers are outside, asking for You.”
But Jesus replied, “Who are My mother and My brothers?”
Looking at those seated in a circle around Him, He said, “Here are My mother and My brothers!
For whoever does the {{thelema|will}} of God is My brother and sister and mother.”

apostolos.gloss: One sent, an envoy or authorized representative. Jesus appoints twelve to be with Him and then to be sent out with His own authority to preach and cast out demons. The number twelve deliberately echoes the twelve tribes, marking the reconstitution of God's people around Jesus.

ischyros.gloss: Strong, mighty, powerful. The strong man is Satan, secure in his house until a stronger One comes. Jesus' exorcisms are not collusion with the devil but the plundering of his house, proof that the stronger One has arrived to bind him.

blasphemia.gloss: Slander, reviling, blasphemy, especially speech that insults God. To blaspheme the Holy Spirit is to look at the Spirit's undeniable work in Jesus and call it the devil's, a settled, hardened rejection of the only One who brings forgiveness, and so it cannot be forgiven.

thelema.gloss: Will, desire, purpose. Doing the will of God, receiving and following Jesus, is what marks out His true family. Kinship in the kingdom is defined not by blood but by glad obedience to the Father.

basic.context: Jesus heals a man's withered hand on the Sabbath, exposing the leaders' hard hearts, and they immediately begin plotting to kill Him. Crowds swarm Him from every region. He goes up a mountain and appoints twelve apostles to be with Him and to be sent out. Then two verdicts land: His own family think He has lost His mind, and the Jerusalem scribes say He is driving out demons by the devil. Jesus shows the charge is absurd, He is the stronger One binding Satan, warns about blaspheming the Spirit, and says His real family is whoever does God's will.
basic.hermeneutics: Notice the pattern of insiders and outsiders. The crowds, the family, and the scribes all misread Jesus, while the Twelve are drawn close and the circle of hearers becomes His family. The warning about the unforgivable sin is not about a careless word but a settled, defiant rejection that calls God's Spirit satanic.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus appoints the twelve apostolos, sent ones, to represent Him. He is the stronger One who ties up the ischyros, the strong man, Satan, and plunders his house. To call His work demonic is to blasphemia, blaspheme, the Holy Spirit. And His true family are those who do the thelema, the will, of God.
basic.typology: The twelve apostles correspond to the twelve tribes of Israel; Jesus is founding a renewed people of God around Himself. Binding the strong man fulfils the promise that the seed of the woman would crush the serpent, and looks ahead to the final defeat of Satan.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Lord of the Sabbath who does good on it, the stronger One who binds Satan, the head of a renewed people, and the one whose family is defined by obedience to God. Even the demons confess Him the Son of God.
basic.god: God's will is the dividing line: those who do it belong to Jesus. God's Spirit is at work in Jesus' every deliverance, so to name that work satanic is to set oneself against God Himself.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 3:15 promises the crushing of the serpent. Isaiah 49:24-25 speaks of plunder taken from the mighty. Hebrews 2:14 says Jesus came to destroy the devil.
basic.oneStory: The war declared in Eden reaches a decisive stage. The stronger One has come to bind the strong man and plunder his house, gathering a renewed Israel around Himself, twelve apostles for twelve tribes. Membership in this new family is open to all who do the will of God, and the story presses on toward the cross where Satan's house is finally overthrown.

context.literary:
Mark 3 is built like a set of nested frames. It closes a run of five conflict stories that began at Mark 2:1 and ends, at 3:6, with the first plot to kill Jesus. A short summary then draws the camera back, 3:7-12, to show a whole nation converging on Him. At the centre stands the appointing of the Twelve, 3:13-19, the one scene on a mountain and the one where Jesus takes the initiative: He calls 'those He wanted.' After that the chapter folds in on itself. Mark does his favourite thing and sandwiches one story inside another. His family goes out to seize Him, 3:20-21, the scribes accuse Him, 3:22-30, and then the family arrives, 3:31-35. The outer story is Jesus' relatives; the inner one is the charge of Satanic power. Mark wants each interpreted by the other, so that the family's verdict, 'He is out of His mind,' is read beside the scribes' verdict, 'He is possessed.'

Inside the sandwich, the argument is tight. Verses 23 to 26 make three conditional statements in a row, kingdom, house, Satan, each ending with the phrase 'cannot stand.' Verse 27 then gives the true account in one image, and verses 28 to 30 draw the sober consequence. The chapter's two uses of the same Greek participle for Jesus 'looking around,' in 3:5 at the hard-hearted and in 3:34 at those seated in a circle, bracket the whole movement. The same eyes that meet hardness with anger and sorrow meet obedience with a family.

Notice too where the Twelve sit. Their appointment is placed between the crowd's frenzy and the family's misunderstanding, and the list of names itself is part of the design. Mark begins with Simon and ends with the man who 'betrayed' Jesus, so the story of failure is announced before it begins. The surrounding material answers the question the chapter keeps pressing: who belongs with Jesus, and who stands outside?
context.historical:
The geography in 3:7-8 is a map of Jewish hopes. Galilee, Judea and Jerusalem are the heartland. Idumea lay to the south and had been forcibly brought into Judaism generations earlier, and Herod's family came from there. The region beyond the Jordan and the vicinity of Tyre and Sidon sit on the margins, partly Gentile territory. People from every direction are coming, and the line of Jesus' influence runs well outside the borders the Pharisees were guarding.

The Sabbath conflict belongs to a real debate. Sabbath rest was one of the great badges of Jewish identity, set in the Ten Commandments, Exodus 20:8-11. Rabbinic texts that were written down after this period allowed Sabbath work to save a life in immediate danger but not ordinary treatment of a chronic condition. A withered hand was not an emergency, which explains why the watchers expected to catch Him. Jesus reframes the question from permitted work to the purpose of the day: do good or do harm, save life or kill. The unusual partners at 3:6, Pharisees and Herodians, show how threatened both groups felt. The Herodians were supporters of the family of Herod, whose rule depended on Rome, and they appear again with the Pharisees at Mark 12:13. Pharisees and a political party meeting at once to plot is a sign of how serious the matter had become.

The scribes who had 'come down from Jerusalem' arrive as a kind of inspection party, since Jerusalem was the centre of the legal and priestly establishment. The name Beelzebul is a title drawn from the old Canaanite storm god Baal, and in the Old Testament a god of Ekron called Baal-zebub is consulted in 2 Kings 1:2. By the first century it had become a name for the prince of demons. Jesus' own relatives mattered in an honour and shame culture, where a son who embarrassed the family was something the household had to deal with. Their move to 'take custody' was a mixture of concern and damage control.

The number twelve would have been heard at once. A people whose identity was twelve tribes, and who had lost ten of them to Assyrian exile, were being shown a new beginning.
context.canonical:
The Twelve are rooted in the structure of Israel. Jacob had twelve sons, and at Sinai Moses built twelve pillars for the twelve tribes, Exodus 24:4. Prophets had promised that God would gather the scattered tribes again, Ezekiel 37:15-22, and Jesus appoints twelve on a mountain, the place where God formed His people before. He later tells them they will sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel, Matthew 19:28 and Luke 22:30. After Judas fails, the apostles ask for his place to be refilled, Acts 1:15-26, because the number matters. At the end of the Bible the New Jerusalem has twelve gates for the tribes and twelve foundations for the apostles of the Lamb, Revelation 21:12-14.

The strong man image reaches back to Isaiah 49:24-25, where the plunder of a mighty tyrant is taken from him because the LORD Himself contends for His people. Isaiah 53:12 sees a servant who will divide the spoils with the strong. In the New Testament the same picture runs on: Jesus says in Luke 11:20-22 that the finger of God is at work and that the stronger man overcomes the armed one and divides his spoils. Colossians 2:15 speaks of the powers disarmed at the cross, and Hebrews 2:14 says the devil's power over death is destroyed.

The warning about blasphemy is repeated in Matthew 12:31-32, which adds 'in this age or in the age to come,' and in Luke 12:10. It is often discussed beside Hebrews 6:4-6 and 10:26-29, which also describe a deliberate rejection from which there is no further sacrifice to appeal to.

The redefinition of family has deep echoes. Jesus' own brothers do not believe in Him according to John 7:5, yet after the resurrection they are with the believers, Acts 1:14, and James becomes a leader of the church in Jerusalem, Galatians 1:19 and 1 Corinthians 15:7. Later Jesus on the cross entrusts His mother to the beloved disciple, John 19:26-27. The picture of God's people as a family of brothers and sisters runs through Romans 8:29 and Hebrews 2:11.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Mark wrote for readers who were learning that following Jesus can cost them their families and their standing. He gives them a Jesus who was himself misread by those closest to Him. The sandwich of 3:20-35 is a pastoral gift: it shows that being thought mad by relatives and demonic by experts is not a sign that Jesus' followers have gone wrong, because Jesus Himself was called both.

Mark also wanted to say what makes a follower. The Twelve are not chosen for talent or purity, and the list even names a traitor. They are appointed first 'to accompany Him' and only then 'to be sent out.' Being with Him comes before doing for Him. The final scene makes the same point from the other side: those seated around Him, listening, are the family, and the people standing outside, even His mother, are invited to come in.

The warning at 3:28-30 is meant to protect, not to terrify. Mark ends it with his own explanation, 'because they were saying, "He has an unclean spirit."' He is telling readers exactly what the sin is, a settled verdict that the work of the Spirit in Jesus is demonic, so that sensitive believers do not carry fears that do not belong to them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records what happened to Jesus and what He said to those who attacked Him. The appointing of exactly twelve is a description of a unique, once-for-all foundation. No one now is appointed to that office, and the passage does not command churches to have twelve of anything. What carries forward is the pattern: Jesus calls people to Himself first and sends them second.

His words about the family are a statement of priority, not a rule that believers should treat their parents and siblings carelessly. Elsewhere He rebukes those who use religious language to avoid caring for their parents, Mark 7:10-13, and from the cross He makes sure His mother is cared for, John 19:26-27. The saying places loyalty to God above even the closest tie.

The claim that Jesus binds the strong man is a description of what He has done in His ministry and will complete at the cross. It is not a technique for believers to bind Satan by formula. And the unforgivable sin is described, not prescribed. The text names a particular act, not a thing a believer can slip into by a bad thought.

debates.question: Is the 'He is out of His mind' of verse 21 said by Jesus' family, or by the crowd?

views.label: The family says it
views.case: The phrase 'His own,' hoi par' autou, can mean relatives, and verses 31 to 35 bring His mother and brothers to the door right after verse 21, so the sandwich pairs them with the scribes. This is how most translations, including the BSB, read it, and it fits Mark's pattern of showing that those closest to Jesus misjudge Him.

views.label: Followers or neighbours from the house
views.case: The phrase is loose enough to mean 'those around Him,' and some see it as friends or neighbours who thought His pace would burn Him out. The case rests on the wide range of the phrase and on the fact that Mark names the family only at verse 31.

debates.bearing: The family reading is the most natural, since Mark himself connects the two scenes. Either way, the chapter shows that devotion to Jesus can look like madness to people who love us, and that love can fail to understand.

debates.question: Who are Jesus' 'brothers,' and does verse 35 say anything about them?

views.label: Natural children of Mary and Joseph
views.case: The plain sense of 'brothers' with Mary, Mark 3:31 and 6:3, is that these were sons born to Mary and Joseph after Jesus. Matthew 1:25 says Joseph did not know Mary 'until she gave birth to a son,' and Luke calls Jesus her 'firstborn,' Luke 2:7. Most Protestants hold this view.

views.label: Half-brothers, sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage
views.case: Some early Christian tradition said Joseph had been married before, so these are his children and Mary remained a virgin. This is the view of much Eastern Christian tradition and rests on later writings rather than on Mark.

views.label: Cousins or close kin
views.case: Jerome argued the Greek word can cover relatives broadly, as the Old Testament uses 'brother' for kinsmen, Genesis 13:8, and that Mary remained a virgin for life. This is the view of much Western Catholic tradition.

debates.bearing: The identity of these men does not change what the saying teaches. The sharper point is that whoever they were, they stood outside the door and later came in, Acts 1:14.

debates.question: Can a believer commit the unforgivable sin by accident or in a bad moment?

views.label: No, it is a settled, deliberate stance
views.case: Mark ties it to verse 30: they were saying Jesus has an unclean spirit. Those who fear they have committed it show by that fear that they have not turned their backs, and the verse that begins the saying, 'all sins and blasphemies' will be forgiven, shows how wide mercy is.

views.label: A one-time historical sin of that generation
views.case: Some say the sin belongs to those who saw Jesus' work in person and still called it Satan's, and cannot be committed in quite the same way after Pentecost. It places weight on the setting of Jesus' earthly ministry.

debates.bearing: On both views the person afraid of this sin is not the person Jesus warns. The danger lies with those who look at the Spirit's work in Jesus and call it evil, and keep calling it that.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the verb in verse 14. The BSB has Jesus 'appointed' twelve, but the Greek underlying it is the plain verb for 'make,' poieo, so that Jesus 'made twelve.' It is the same verb that appears again at verse 35 in 'does the will of God,' poieo. The group is made, and the family is the ones who do. Then comes the purpose clause: they are appointed 'that they might be with Him' and 'that He might send them out.' The Greek is built from two parallel hina clauses, and the order is deliberate. Being with Him is first, the sending is second.

Next, the word for the demons being driven out. The verb in verse 15 is ekballo, the same verb used for driving out in verse 22 and for the Spirit 'driving' Jesus into the wilderness in Mark 1:12. Jesus is not trading in a mild charm. He expels, and the Twelve share that authority, exousia, a word for delegated right rather than personal force.

The word for the 'family' at verse 21 is a phrase, hoi par' autou, literally 'those from beside Him,' and it can cover relatives or close associates. The verb for what they intend, krateo, 'to seize,' is the verb Mark later uses for the arrest of Jesus, 14:1 and 14:44, and for Herod's seizure of John, 6:17. The relatives set out to seize Him as the authorities one day will. And 'out of His mind' is the verb existemi, 'to stand outside oneself.' It is used in 2:12 for the crowd who were 'amazed' at the healed paralytic. In Mark, a response to Jesus that is wonder in one scene is a charge of madness in another.

The accusation of verse 22 uses the name Beelzebul, and it turns on a preposition: 'by the prince of the demons' means 'in' or 'by the power of' him. Jesus' reply uses a nice word at verse 26, 'his end has come,' telos, the same word used elsewhere for a completed goal. Satan's house is not only divided but heading for its finish.

The strong man of verse 27 is ischyros, and the verb for 'ties up,' deo, is the ordinary word for binding. The comparison of the 'stronger One' appears in Mark 1:7, where John said, 'After me comes One more powerful than I,' using the comparative of the same root, ischyroteros. So the Baptist's promise is exactly what is happening here.

The blasphemy saying has a rare phrase, 'eternal sin,' and the verb for 'will never be forgiven' is a strong double negative in the Greek, ouk echei aphesin eis ton aiona, literally 'has no forgiveness for the age.' The same family of words, aphesis, is used for forgiveness throughout the Gospel, so the severity is real.

Finally, in verse 34 Jesus 'looks around' with the verb periblepo, which Mark uses again and again of Jesus, and it is the very verb of verse 5, where it was anger and sorrow. The difference is the object. Here He looks 'in a circle,' kyklo, at those seated around Him, and what He sees is family.

typology.type: The twelve apostles as the twelve tribes
typology.fulfillment: Israel was a people formed around twelve sons, and Moses marked the covenant at Sinai with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes, Exodus 24:4. Jesus climbs a mountain and forms a new group of twelve, which says that the true Israel is gathering around Him. He promises that they will sit on twelve thrones, Matthew 19:28, and the final city has their names on its foundations, Revelation 21:14. The correspondence is real, yet it escalates: the first twelve were born into their place, while these are called by name and sent to the whole world. The type falls short because the tribes were bound by blood and land, while the apostles are bound by the person of Christ.

typology.type: The strong man bound and his house plundered
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 49:24-25 asks whether plunder can be taken from a mighty man and answers that the LORD Himself will take it back for the captives. Jesus applies the picture to His own work: each exorcism is a raid on Satan's house. The binding is begun in the wilderness, Mark 1:12-13, shown in every deliverance, and finished at the cross, where He disarmed the rulers and authorities, Colossians 2:15, and shared in flesh and blood to destroy the devil's hold on death, Hebrews 2:14. The picture is not yet complete: the devil is still active, 1 Peter 5:8, until the last judgment, Revelation 20:10.

typology.type: The man with the withered hand as a sign of Israel's need
typology.fulfillment: A hand that cannot grasp or work stands for a people unable to do what God asked. Jesus commands the man to do the one thing he cannot do, stretch out his hand, and it is restored as he obeys. This echoes the prophets' promise that God would heal and restore His people, Ezekiel 37:1-14. The Gospel does not itself say the withered hand is a symbol, so this is an echo rather than an explicit type. But the pattern is the gospel in small: God's command carries God's power, and the restoration comes in the act of obeying.

typology.type: The family that does God's will, a new household
typology.fulfillment: In the Old Testament, belonging to God's people came by birth, circumcision and covenant, and the household of Israel was one of kinship. Jesus gathers a new household in which those who sit around Him and do God's will are brothers, sisters and mother. This is where Paul goes later: believers are adopted as sons and are 'brothers' of the firstborn, Romans 8:15 and 8:29, and Hebrews 2:11 says Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers. The pattern escalates in that the new family is not limited by blood or ethnicity, Galatians 3:26-29. It falls short of the final picture only in that it is not yet complete: the family still waits for the great gathering, Revelation 7:9.

study.christ:
Chapter 3 is a portrait of the kind of person Jesus is, put in the shape of four reactions to Him. The synagogue shows Him as the Lord of the Sabbath, as 2:28 has just said. The question He asks, whether it is lawful to do good or harm on that day, shows that He treats the Sabbath as God's gift for life, and His anger and sorrow show a Messiah who can be moved by hardness of heart. That sorrow is worth noticing. The strong Son of God is not indifferent; He grieves over people who would rather keep a rule than see a man restored.

He is the stronger One whom John promised, Mark 1:7. The picture of binding the strong man is a claim about who He is. The one who can enter Satan's house and take it apart is not a prophet or a healer but the one who has come in the power of God, Luke 11:20. The demons already know this. They fall before Him and call Him the Son of God, 3:11, and He silences them, not because the title is wrong but because Mark wants the title to be understood at the cross, where a Roman centurion will say it, Mark 15:39.

He is the founder of a new Israel. Choosing twelve is a claim to authority over the people of God. No one but God, or God's anointed, has the right to constitute Israel afresh. The appointment is called out as 'those He wanted,' and in this the Lord's own free choice is on display, recalling Deuteronomy 7:7, where Israel was chosen not for size but because the LORD loved them.

He is the one who redefines kinship. By saying who His family is, He sets Himself at the centre of belonging: to be in the family is to do the will of God as it is made known around Him. He lived this out. In Gethsemane He prays, 'not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39, and Hebrews 10:7 puts on His lips the words of Psalm 40:8, 'I have come to do Your will, O God.' He is the first and pre-eminent member of the family He defines.

Be careful not to flatten the passage. Not every detail is a hidden picture of Jesus. The names of the apostles are not a code, and the withered hand is not a coded sermon. The links above rest on what Mark and the rest of the New Testament say outright.

Finally, the passage looks to the cross. The plot at 3:6 is the first move toward it, and Judas is named as the one who 'betrayed' Him, a word that will return in the passion. The family that came to seize Him and the authorities who will seize Him later have one thing in common: they think they know better than He does. In His death He binds the strong man, and in His resurrection the family expands, as His own brothers, who stood outside, are later found inside, Acts 1:14.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who is sovereign in choosing. 'Those He wanted' is the language of free election, not of recruitment. The Twelve did not apply; they were called, and they came. Deuteronomy 7:7-8 gives the same logic: the LORD set His love on Israel because He loved them, not because they were great. So the first thing the passage teaches about God is that He starts the relationship and defines it.

He is a God who cares more about persons than about the way His own gifts are kept. The Sabbath was His own institution, and Jesus can say with confidence that it was made to do good and to save life. This does not loosen the law. It shows the heart behind it, the same heart that gave the day of rest as a gift to slaves who had never had one, Deuteronomy 5:12-15. God's rules express His character, and His character is life-giving.

He is stronger than evil. The passage never treats the contest between Jesus and Satan as one between equals. The adversary's house is one that can be entered and plundered. The demons tremble, fall down and confess, and Jesus gives the commands. This matters for worship: the God whom we praise does not merely stand against evil but is in the act of overcoming it.

He is Trinitarian in action, though the passage does not use the term. The Spirit is at work in Jesus' ministry, the Son is the stronger One, and the will of God the Father is the thing that defines the family. To blaspheme the Spirit by calling His work satanic is to turn away from the very means by which God draws people to the Son. The Spirit is not a force; the sin is against Him. The grammar of the warning treats Him as a person who can be slandered.

He is also merciful in a very wide way. 'The sons of men will be forgiven all sins and blasphemies' is among the most generous sentences in the Gospel. God's mercy does not run out at some level of badness. The one exception is a refusal of the only source of pardon, and even that is described not as God running out of patience but as a person who will not come.

He holds together holiness and nearness. In Jesus, God comes close to demons, to the sick and to the unclean and is not defiled. At the same time, He tests those who stand near Him. Judas was close. A man can sit in the circle, be named among the Twelve and still turn.

For worship, this means we praise a God who chooses, who is stronger than every enemy, whose Spirit works to turn us to the Son, and who gathers us not as servants only but as family, 'My brother and sister and mother.' We respond not by trying to earn our way in but by sitting down near Him and doing what He says.

crossReferences.note: Moses built an altar and twelve pillars for the twelve tribes at the foot of the mountain when the covenant was sealed. Jesus' choosing of twelve on a mountain in Mark 3:13-14 reads naturally against that scene, showing the people of God being formed around a new mediator.

The prophet asks if plunder can be taken from the mighty and replies that the LORD will contend with those who contend with His people and take it back. Jesus' picture of tying up the strong man and plundering his house fits this promise, with Jesus as the One carrying it out.

Luke's parallel to the strong man saying adds that Jesus drives out demons by 'the finger of God,' recalling Exodus 8:19, and that when a stronger man attacks, he takes away the armor on which the strong man relied. It shows that the exorcisms are signs that the kingdom has arrived.

Matthew's version of the blasphemy saying adds that the sin will not be forgiven 'either in this age or in the age to come.' It confirms that the warning is about a person's final stance toward the Spirit's witness to Jesus, and it sits next to the same charge that Jesus casts out demons by Beelzebul.

John says One more powerful than he is coming. The stronger One of Mark 3:27 is that promised figure. Mark has set up the encounter at the start of his Gospel so that readers will recognise what the binding of the strong man means.

John records that even His brothers did not believe in Him. It is the same situation behind Mark 3:21 and 3:31, the family standing outside, seen from another Gospel. It also makes the later change more striking, when the brothers are found among the believers in Acts 1:14.

After the ascension the apostles are together in prayer with the women, with Mary the mother of Jesus and with His brothers. Those who stood outside the house in Mark 3 are now in the room. The door Jesus held open at 3:34-35 has been walked through.

Jesus tells the Twelve that in the renewal of all things they will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel. It confirms that the number in Mark 3:14 was no accident and that the appointment looks toward the age to come.

David says, 'I delight to do Your will, O my God.' Hebrews 10:5-7 gives these words to Christ at His coming into the world. Jesus is the one who does the will of God perfectly, and He invites others into the family by sharing that obedience.

The one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one Father, and so Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers. This is the finished form of Mark 3:34-35, now explained through His death and resurrection.

The new city's twelve gates carry the names of the twelve tribes and its twelve foundations the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb. The two sets of twelve are joined, giving the end of the story that Mark 3:14 begins.

study.oneStory:
The war that was declared in the garden is now in the open. Genesis 3:15 set a descendant of the woman against the serpent. Mark 3 shows the first real exchange of blows: the strong man's house is entered, and the one who enters is the promised stronger One. Everything in the chapter moves toward that confrontation, and the cross is where the binding will be completed.

The chapter also takes up the story of Israel. Israel began with twelve sons and twelve tribes, was scattered, and was promised restoration. Now Jesus chooses twelve and begins to rebuild the people of God around Himself. The old people is not discarded, because the Twelve are all Jewish and Jesus sends them first to Israel. But the boundary of the family is redrawn. Insiders can turn out to be outside, like the scribes and, for a time, His own relatives, while those who sit and listen are inside.

The theme of family runs through the whole Bible. Adam and Eve were created to fill the earth as one family, Genesis 1:28, and sin scattered it, with Cain killing Abel and Babel dividing the nations, Genesis 4 and 11. God's answer begins with one family, Abraham's, through which 'all the families of the earth will be blessed,' Genesis 12:3. Jesus' words at the house in Capernaum say how this blessing will reach beyond bloodlines: through the will of God done around Him. Paul states the conclusion: those in Christ are Abraham's seed and heirs, Galatians 3:29, adopted as children, Romans 8:15-17.

It also faces the problem of the heart. The Pharisees watching for an accusation and the scribes inspecting Jesus show that the greatest barrier to God's kingdom is not ignorance but a stubborn will that sees a gift and names it a threat. Mark's 'hardness of heart' recurs for the disciples too, 6:52 and 8:17, so nobody is outside the problem. The story needs a rescuer who deals with the heart as well as the demons.

The new creation completes the picture. The final city has the tribes and the apostles together, Revelation 21:12-14, and the people of God are drawn from every nation, tribe, people and language, Revelation 7:9. The family that began around one table in a crowded house in Capernaum fills a city, and the enemy that was bound in part is thrown at last into the lake of fire, Revelation 20:10. There will be no more curse, and God Himself will dwell with His people, Revelation 21:3.

quiz.q: What did Jesus expose by healing the withered hand on the Sabbath?

options.text: That doing good and saving life is what the Sabbath is for, while His opponents' hard hearts preferred to plot evil.
options.note: Mark 3:4-6 sets Jesus' question about doing good against the leaders' murderous hardness.

options.text: That He was willing to work on the Sabbath.
options.note: He did heal on the Sabbath, but the deeper exposure was the leaders' hardness and His teaching that the day is for doing good.

options.text: That the man's faith was greater than the crowd's.
options.note: The focus is not the man's faith but the lawfulness of doing good and the leaders' hearts.

options.text: That the Sabbath law had never mattered to God.
options.note: Jesus upholds the Sabbath's true purpose rather than dismissing it.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus appoint twelve apostles?

options.text: To be with Him and to be sent out with His authority, forming a renewed people echoing the twelve tribes.
options.note: Mark 3:14-15 states their purpose; the number twelve signals a reconstituted Israel.

options.text: To be with Him and to be sent out to preach and cast out demons.
options.note: Correct about their commission, but it misses the deeper significance of the number twelve for a renewed Israel.

options.text: To manage the crowds that pressed around Him.
options.note: A boat handled the crowds; the Twelve were appointed for mission, not crowd control.

options.text: To replace the priests in the temple.
options.note: The Twelve were sent to preach and deliver, not to serve as temple priests.

quiz.q: How does Jesus answer the charge that He casts out demons by the devil?

options.text: Satan cannot drive out Satan; rather, Jesus is the stronger One who binds the strong man and plunders his house.
options.note: Mark 3:23-27 gives both the logic and the strong-man image.

options.text: A kingdom divided against itself cannot stand.
options.note: True and part of His answer, but incomplete without the claim to be the stronger One binding Satan.

options.text: He simply denied doing any exorcisms.
options.note: He does not deny the exorcisms; He explains their true source and meaning.

options.text: He admitted using Beelzebul's power for good ends.
options.note: He flatly rejects the charge; His power is the Spirit's, not the devil's.

quiz.q: What is the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit in this passage?

options.text: A settled, defiant labelling of the Spirit's work in Jesus as demonic, a hardened rejection of the only source of forgiveness.
options.note: Verse 30 ties it to their claim that He has an unclean spirit; it is a hardened rejection, not a single slip.

options.text: Speaking any careless word against the Holy Spirit.
options.note: It is more than a careless word; it is a persistent, clear-eyed rejection of the Spirit's testimony to Christ.

options.text: Doubting whether Jesus really performed miracles.
options.note: Honest doubt is not the unforgivable sin; the sin is calling the Spirit's evident work satanic.

options.text: Any sin committed after conversion.
options.note: Jesus says all other sins and blasphemies can be forgiven; this is a specific, hardened rejection.

quiz.q: Who does Jesus say are His true mother and brothers?

options.text: Whoever does the will of God is His brother and sister and mother.
options.note: Mark 3:35 defines His true family by obedience to God.

options.text: Those who sit near Him and listen to His teaching.
options.note: He gestures to the listeners, but the defining mark He names is doing God's will, not mere proximity.

options.text: Only His biological mother and brothers from Nazareth.
options.note: Jesus deliberately widens the family beyond blood ties to all who do God's will.

options.text: Only the twelve apostles.
options.note: The family is open to whoever does God's will, not the Twelve alone.

questions: Jesus was grieved at hard hearts that would rather plot than rejoice at a healing. Where might your own heart be hardening toward what God is doing?
The Twelve were appointed first to be with Jesus and then to be sent. How does being with Him shape and fuel the ways you are sent into the world?
The scribes saw undeniable good and called it evil. How can you guard against a cynicism that explains away the clear work of God?
Jesus binds the strong man and plunders his house. How does knowing that Satan is already being overpowered change the way you face spiritual struggle?
Jesus' true family is defined by doing God's will. What would it look like this week to belong to Jesus not by label but by glad obedience?

translationNotes.note: Some manuscripts do not include the phrase whom He designated as apostles; the meaning is unaffected, since the Twelve are plainly sent out with Jesus' authority.
His family, literally those with Him or His own people, went out to take custody of Him, convinced He was beside Himself; Mark frames this alongside the scribes' harsher charge.
Guilty of eternal sin translates a phrase meaning liable to a sin that has no end of guilt; the context, verse 30, defines it as calling the Holy Spirit's work an unclean spirit's.
